title: Launch brief (draft) — Private Observability Minimum Pack
content:
Doc purpose
This is the launch brief draft for Redwood Private “Observability Minimum Pack” (a baseline, supported observability bundle for VPC + on-prem installs). This doc is intended for Product/Eng/SRE/Support to align on: (1) messaging and definition of “supported” installs, (2) release timing + rollout plan, (3) support readiness checklist, and (4) upgrade notes / known pitfalls.

Owner: Vivek Kulkarni (Product — Private Deployments)
Program: Talia Benson
Last edited: 2025-08-05

1) What we’re launching
Name
Private Observability Minimum Pack (a.k.a. “minimum pack”, “min pack”).

One-liner
A turnkey, supported set of dashboards, alerts, and log collection defaults that ships with Redwood Private so customers (and Redwood Support/SRE) can reliably monitor health and performance without bespoke setup.

Problem statement
Private installs are inconsistent in what signals exist (and how) across customer environments (VPC and on-prem). This creates:
- Longer time-to-triage for incidents and escalations
- Higher variance in what Support can reasonably troubleshoot
- Misaligned customer expectations (“I installed Private; why are there no Redwood dashboards?”)
- Avoidable churn risk for regulated customers where instrumentation + SIEM export is a hard requirement

What is included in v1
Dashboards (Grafana)
- Runtime overview: golden signals (rate/errors/latency), token throughput, batching/queueing, GPU utilization, and common saturation indicators
- Control plane health: API gateway, policy/routing, auth integration points, rollout/upgrade controller
- Infrastructure essentials: scrape health, exporter status, resource pressure indicators (CPU/mem/storage) where available

Alerts (Prometheus)
- Latency/availability: SLO burn-style alerts (where recording rules exist), plus pragmatic symptom alerts for common failure modes
- GPU saturation / OOM / restart loops: page-worthy alerts scoped to inference namespaces with noise controls
- Prometheus scrape health: alerts to catch “we are blind” conditions (targets down / series churn)

Logs (collection + export)
- Baseline log collector configuration for Private control plane + data plane components
- Structured logging expectations and safe defaults (redaction guidance; no request payload logging by default)
- Supported export options (documented, tested configs):
  - Splunk HEC (priority)
  - Elasticsearch/OpenSearch
  - Loki (where applicable / customer-provided)
  - OTLP logs (document as “best-effort / validate with customer”, unless validated by GA)

Packaging / install surfaces
- Wired into `redwood-helm-charts` with versioned values and feature toggles
- Integrated into `redwood-private-installer`:
  - preflight checks (storage/network/resources)
  - post-install validation (scrapes, dashboards present)
- Air-gapped bundle includes dashboards/rules/log configs and required images (per bundle manifest)

What is NOT included (explicit non-goals for v1)
- “Premium” observability features: long retention, multi-cluster federation, full tracing rollouts with sampling UI, custom per-customer dashboards
- Building a new in-house SIEM
- Unlimited label cardinality / per-tenant dashboards (we will cap/aggregate for Private safety)

2) Definition of “supported” (messaging + policy)
Messaging principle
“Supported” means: if the customer installs Redwood Private using the documented installer/Helm pathways, with the minimum pack enabled and no unsupported modifications, Redwood can:
- validate that key signals exist (scrapes, dashboards render, alerts evaluate)
- use those signals for Support/SRE triage
- provide a bounded set of configuration guidance (retention, resource sizing, export targets)

Supported environments
- Kubernetes-based Redwood Private deployments in:
  - VPC/private cloud
  - on-prem, including air-gapped installs (when using the offline bundle)

Supported observability stack assumptions
We are not forcing customers to replace their stack. However, “minimum supported” assumes:
- Prometheus-compatible scraping is available (customer Prometheus or Redwood-provided Prometheus in the chart, depending on install mode)
- Grafana is available (customer Grafana or packaged Grafana)
- Log collection daemonset/agent is installed per chart defaults (or documented equivalent) and can forward to an approved sink

Supported vs customer-owned responsibilities (copy for docs)
- Redwood owns: metrics emitted by Redwood components, dashboards/alerts we ship, defaults we provide, installer validation, doc + runbooks.
- Customer owns: cluster sizing, storage class, network policies, Grafana SSO/auth configuration, SIEM endpoint availability, and any non-default modifications.

What counts as “unsupported modifications” (examples)
- Removing required metrics endpoints or blocking scrape paths without equivalents
- Renaming namespaces/labels without applying the documented overrides
- Aggressive retention/storage settings that cause TSDB churn or data loss without following guidance

3) Positioning and customer-facing messaging
Primary audience
- Customer platform/infra teams operating Private installs
- Security/compliance stakeholders (logging export + redaction/retention)
- Redwood Support + SRE (triage + escalation readiness)

Key value props (customer-facing)
- Faster time-to-triage: standard dashboards + alerts that Redwood Support knows how to use
- Safety defaults: bounded metric cardinality, redaction guidance, and “no payload logging” by default
- Works in constrained environments: supports air-gapped packaging and common SIEM exports
- Upgrade-safe: versioned artifacts and installer checks to reduce “dashboards disappeared” and “alerts got noisy” scenarios

Suggested copy (external-ish; can be adapted)
“Redwood Private now includes a Minimum Observability Pack: a supported baseline of Grafana dashboards, Prometheus alerts, and structured log collection defaults. It’s designed for secure VPC and on‑prem environments (including air‑gapped) so your team can monitor latency, errors, throughput, and resource saturation out of the box—and so Redwood Support can help you troubleshoot quickly when you need it.”

What to avoid saying
- Don’t claim “full observability parity with hosted” (we have known parity gaps)
- Don’t imply tracing is GA unless we validate OTLP end-to-end in reference environments
- Don’t promise “no alert noise”; instead promise “curated + severity-mapped + tunable defaults”

4) Release plan / timing (draft)
Target release
- Target: Private release train 2025.09 (or next available Private GA patch train depending on branch cut)
- Beta window: 2–3 weeks prior in staging reference environments + 1–2 design partners (VPC + on-prem)

Rollout strategy
- Phase 0: internal validation (CI + staging)
  - smoke tests green (dashboards render; scrapes present; synthetic failure triggers at least one alert)
- Phase 1: limited external (design partners)
  - confirm:
    - on-prem airgap bundle completeness
    - Splunk HEC export works with real enterprise constraints
    - no high-cardinality regressions under realistic load
- Phase 2: GA
  - docs published
  - Support enabled
  - release notes included

Backward/forward compatibility stance
- Dashboards and alerts are versioned with the Private release.
- Metric naming migrations must be:
  - backward compatible for at least one minor version, OR
  - accompanied by a clear migration doc and installer notes.

5) Support readiness checklist (must be true before GA)
Support enablement
[ ] Support playbook published (triage path: “no dashboards”, “no metrics”, “alerts noisy”, “log export failing”)
[ ] Known issues page created and linked from docs
[ ] Runbook links embedded in alert annotations (first 2–3 steps + escalation guidance)
[ ] Support training session scheduled (30–45 min) + recording posted
[ ] Escalation owners defined (Platform Telemetry, SRE, Private Deployments)

Operational readiness
[ ] Default dashboards installed and visible with a fresh Private install (VPC)
[ ] Default dashboards installed and visible with an air-gapped install
[ ] Prometheus scrape targets are automatically discovered OR explicitly documented to be added
[ ] Post-install validation flags missing datasources/scrapes as actionable errors
[ ] Alert severities mapped to paging policy (page vs ticket) and reviewed by SRE
[ ] “Noisy alerts” list identified + defaults set conservatively (some alerts disabled by default if needed)

Security / compliance readiness
[ ] Security review completed for structured logs (no secrets/PII; no payload logging)
[ ] Redaction guidance documented (what we redact, what customers should avoid)
[ ] Retention defaults documented and safe for regulated workloads (customer-configurable)
[ ] Audit log interaction clarified (audit logs ≠ operational logs; both have separate retention guidance)

Customer success readiness
[ ] FAQ for enterprise prospects: SIEM export options + airgap details
[ ] Reference architecture diagram(s) available (at least “typical VPC” and “typical on-prem”)

Engineering quality gates
[ ] CI: private observability smoke tests passing on main release branch
[ ] Installer preflight checks validated on constrained clusters (small storage class, restricted NetworkPolicies)
[ ] Helm values documented, including minimal overrides for:
    - existing customer Prometheus/Grafana
    - existing log forwarder
[ ] Sizing guidance published (Prometheus/Grafana/log collector resources and PVC)

6) Upgrade notes (draft content for release notes + docs)
Top upgrade risks we are addressing
- Dashboards “disappearing” after upgrade
  - Root causes observed: dashboard sidecar not running, missing ConfigMaps, Grafana datasource rename, or RBAC changes.
  - Mitigation: installer post-upgrade validation + clearer Helm values; dashboard bundle version pinned.

- Alerts suddenly becoming noisy
  - Root causes: threshold defaults too tight for customer footprints, or metric cardinality spikes causing evaluation jitter.
  - Mitigation: severity review + conservative defaults; clear tuning knobs; cardinality caps.

- Prometheus scrapes failing due to NetworkPolicy tightening
  - Root causes: customer policies blocking scrape ports/paths.
  - Mitigation: preflight check detects blocked scrapes and prints required allowlist rules; docs include NetworkPolicy examples.

- Log forwarder backpressure / dropping
  - Root causes: sink unreachable, auth errors, insufficient buffers, or high-volume debug logging.
  - Mitigation: default batch/backoff settings; guidance on durability vs resource usage; “turn down debug” guidance.

Upgrade instructions (high level)
- Before upgrade:
  - snapshot Grafana dashboards (if customer customized locally)
  - verify Prometheus storage has headroom (PVC + retention)
  - confirm SIEM endpoint credentials and connectivity
- During upgrade:
  - keep observability pack version aligned with Private release (do not mix versions unless directed)
- After upgrade:
  - run installer/Helm post-install validation steps
  - confirm:
    - Prometheus targets up for Redwood components
    - Redwood dashboards present and rendering
    - at least one alert rule group loaded
    - log sink receiving events (basic sanity query)

Migration / breaking change policy (to include in docs)
- If a metric name or label set changes, we will:
  - include recording rules to preserve old series for at least one release where feasible, and/or
  - ship updated dashboards in the same release, and
  - call it out explicitly in upgrade notes.

7) Release notes blurb (draft)
“Redwood Private now ships with an Observability Minimum Pack: a supported baseline of Grafana dashboards, Prometheus alert rules, and log collection defaults for Private installs (VPC and on-prem, including air‑gapped). The pack provides runtime and control plane dashboards (latency, error rate, throughput, GPU saturation, queueing/backpressure), curated alerts mapped to severity, and documented log export integrations (e.g., Splunk HEC and Elasticsearch/OpenSearch).”

8) FAQ (internal use; may be adapted)
Q: Do customers need to use the packaged Prometheus/Grafana?
A: No. We support customer-provided Prometheus/Grafana as long as the scrape/datasource configuration matches the documented expectations. The installer/Helm values include a “bring-your-own” pathway.

Q: Is tracing included?
A: Not as a GA promise in v1. We’ll document traces as “where feasible” and avoid positioning it as part of the minimum supported baseline unless validated end-to-end in reference environments.

Q: What does “supported” mean for Splunk/ELK exports?
A: We provide tested configuration templates + troubleshooting steps for supported sinks. We don’t own the customer’s SIEM availability, indexing limits, or credential management, but Support can use the playbooks to diagnose common integration failures.

Q: Will this increase cluster cost?
A: Some additional resource usage is expected for scraping, dashboards, and log collection. We will publish sizing guidance and defaults tuned for small/medium Private footprints with clear knobs for retention and buffer sizes.

9) Open items / decisions needed
- Confirm GA release train (2025.09 vs earlier patch train)
- Confirm which alert rules are enabled by default vs opt-in (based on latest noise review)
- Confirm OTLP log export is “supported” vs “best-effort” for v1
- Finalize: “supported stack” wording (avoid implying we require Grafana/Prometheus vendor X)
- Finalize: default retention guidance (metrics + logs) for regulated customers

10) Internal comms plan (draft)
- #eng-private-deployments: weekly status + readiness checklist updates
- #support: 30-min enablement + playbook walkthrough 1–2 weeks before GA
- Release coordination: confirm branch cut + backport requirements; ensure docs merge by RC

Appendix: Suggested artifacts to link from final launch brief
- Confluence: Private Observability Minimum Pack Overview
- Confluence: Day-2 ops runbook (verify scrapes/dashboards, common failure modes)
- Confluence: Known issues and workarounds
- Confluence: Metrics/alerting standards for Private
- Docs: install + configuration examples (Splunk HEC, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch)

Changelog
- 2025-08-05: Added explicit definition of “supported”, expanded support readiness checklist, and drafted upgrade risk section.
- 2025-07-10: Initial draft created (outline + early messaging).
